📌 Governance Snapshots: Why Your Tokens May Not Count in a DAO Vote

Main Points
⏺ Some DAOs calculate voting power using token balances from a specific blockchain block
⏺ Buying tokens after that snapshot may not increase your voting power
⏺ This post explains how balance snapshots work and why purchase timing matters

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol records balances at a selected block to determine how many votes each participant receives.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — a fixed reference point prevents voting power from changing every time tokens are transferred during the voting process.
3️⃣ Example — a vote uses balances from block #1000, but you buy tokens at block #1005. Those new tokens won't increase your voting power for that proposal.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — users may buy governance tokens specifically to participate, only to discover the snapshot already happened.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before buying governance tokens, check the snapshot block, delegation conditions, and voting eligibility rules.

Final Thoughts

DAO governance isn't only about how many tokens you hold. It can also depend on when you held them. Sometimes your voting power is decided before the vote even begins.

⚠️ South Korea demands stronger crypto safeguards following Binance hack 

⭐️ South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has directed domestic cryptocurrency exchanges to hold more assets in cold wallets and strengthen their financial reserves following the $6.3 billion Binance hack on October 29. The meeting was chaired by Yu Young-jun, the FSC’s director of digital finance policy, and included representatives from the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Security Institute and the Digital Asset eXchange Alliance (DAXA).

❗️ Officials examined how domestic exchanges manage access to their internal systems, approve cryptocurrency withdrawals and control administrator privileges. Exchanges were subsequently asked to strengthen their security procedures, maintain additional reserves and prepare for suspicious transactions or unauthorized access attempts. Under South Korea’s Virtual Asset User Protection Act, cryptocurrency service providers must already hold at least 80% of customers’ deposited digital assets in cold wallets, which remain disconnected from the internet.

📊 The FSC has now asked exchanges to raise their cold storage ratios beyond their existing levels, although the regulator did not announce a new uniform minimum during the meeting. As of the end of September, Upbit held 99.17% of customer assets in cold storage, followed by Bithumb at 94.76% and Coinone at 85%. DigitalEx and GOPAX reported ratios of 82.79% and 80.54%, respectively.

Supreme Court Blocks Trump’s Bid to Set Aside California Ballots ⚖️🗳


The U.S. Supreme Court has rejected an emergency request from the Trump administration seeking to force California to set aside more than 20,000 mail-in ballots ahead of Tuesday’s crucial midterm elections. The decision marks another legal setback for the White House in its escalating effort to challenge voter eligibility and influence election procedures across the country.

In an unsigned order issued Monday, November 2, the justices declined to intervene in the dispute, leaving lower-court decisions against the administration in place. The court offered no explanation for its ruling, and none of the justices publicly dissented. The Justice Department had argued that California should temporarily separate ballots cast by voters whom federal officials suspected of being noncitizens. 

According to the administration, the disputed ballots could no longer be identified once mixed with other votes, making it impossible to verify the eligibility of the individuals who cast them. Federal officials maintained that their database identified thousands of people who might not be U.S. citizens but were nevertheless registered to vote. 

They sought judicial intervention before the ballots were counted, arguing that allowing the process to continue would make it impossible to correct potential violations. California officials strongly challenged the federal government's claims, questioning both the accuracy of the database and the legality of the proposed intervention. State authorities argued that the federal lists contained significant errors and could wrongly identify American citizens as ineligible voters.

Independent researchers also raised concerns about the reliability of the information. Their review found that approximately 9,000 names on the federal list did not appear on California's voter registration rolls. Other cases involved personal identifying details that matched individuals who were U.S. citizens.

Opponents of the administration's request warned that separating thousands of ballots based on questionable data could disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine confidence in the electoral process. They also argued that federal authorities were attempting to interfere with election procedures traditionally administered by state governments.

The Supreme Court's decision follows a series of defeats for the Trump administration in lower courts. Federal judges had previously rejected attempts to delay or block the counting of the disputed ballots, citing concerns over the legal basis for the government's demands and the potential harm to legitimate voters. The case has become part of a broader confrontation between the Justice Department and several states over voter registration, election administration and the federal government's authority to challenge voting procedures.

The administration has pursued similar legal challenges elsewhere, seeking access to voter records and questioning the eligibility of individuals identified through federal databases. 

Critics argue that inaccurate allegations of widespread noncitizen voting risk creating confusion, intimidating election officials and discouraging eligible citizens from participating. With the midterm elections approaching, Monday's ruling leaves California's election authorities free to proceed without the ballot-segregation order sought by the White House.
